title: English Vocabulary in Use — Elementary · Units 29–30 (editorial revision)
description: Units 29–30 reviewed against the textbook teaching pages, maps, illustrations, signs, exercises and British-English phonemic index; all learning notes and examples are in English.
sourceNotice: Source vocabulary and learning objectives follow the user-provided Cambridge textbook. Example sentences and editorial explanations are original; copyrighted textbook exercises and illustrations are not reproduced.

audit.scope: Unit 29: illustrated places and shop/service functions, five urban signs, town map and asking/giving directions, exercises 29.1–29.6. Unit 30: countryside landscape diagram, village/farm/cottage contrasts, nature/conservation and article-use warnings, countryside activities and exercises 30.1–30.5.
audit.pronunciation: British English IPA was checked against the textbook phonemic index (PDF pages 160–170) for indexed headwords. Other inflected words and longer phrases were reviewed compositionally; independent dictionary confirmation is not claimed.
audit.cannotGuarantee: JSON syntax, required fields, ID stability and static source-coverage checks do not verify real browser import, pronunciation or listening exercises, speech synthesis, adaptive progress, or backup and restoration. Human editorial approval remains outstanding.

editorialReview.reviewMethod: Direct inspection of textbook illustrations, notices, map and exercise diagrams on four corresponding PDF pages; item-by-item editorial review and source-index IPA checks where listed; automated JSON, type, language policy and ID-preservation tests.
editorialReview.notes: All pre-existing package, unit and item IDs are unchanged. Extra exercise-linked expressions use unique new IDs. Browser-level import, TTS, progress preservation, and backup and restore remain untested.

units.title: Unit 29 — In the town
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use Elementary, 3rd ed., Unit 29, textbook pp. 64–65 (PDF pp. 65–66); original example sentences.

items.example: The train station is near the river.
items.note: A train station is a place to catch trains. Railway station is also usual in British English.

items.example: We met outside the railway station.
items.note: Railway station and train station have the same meaning. The textbook labels both as places to catch trains.

items.example: You can catch a bus to London from the bus station.
items.note: A bus station is where many bus services start or finish their routes. A bus stop is usually smaller.

items.example: There is a small shop near the station.
items.note: A shop is a place where you buy things; its plural is shops. Store is also common, particularly in American English.

items.example: There are several shops near my office.
items.note: Shops is the plural of shop. The textbook uses this plural for the shopping facilities in a town.

items.example: The shopping centre closes at nine.
items.note: A shopping centre is an area with many shops. Centre is the British spelling; American English uses center.

items.example: Ask for a town map at the tourist information office.
items.note: Tourists can ask for information and local maps here. Information is an uncountable noun.

items.example: The museum has an exhibition about the town.
items.note: A museum displays interesting objects, often old ones. Visit a museum or see exhibits in a museum.

items.example: There is a bank opposite the museum.
items.note: In this unit, a bank is a place where you can change money or use a cash machine.

items.example: I need to visit the post office today.
items.note: A post office is where you can send or post letters and parcels. Do not confuse it with a shop.

items.example: I borrowed a book from the library.
items.note: You can read or borrow books from a library. A bookshop sells books; it is not a library.

items.example: The town hall is in the main square.
items.note: A town hall is the building where local-government officers work.

items.example: There is a car park behind the shops.
items.note: A British English term for a place to park cars; parking lot is usual in American English.

items.example: Cars cannot enter the pedestrian area.
items.note: An area where people can walk but where cars are generally not allowed. Pedestrian refers to a person on foot.

items.example: I got some cash from the cash machine.
items.note: A cash machine lets you withdraw money. ATM is another common term in British and American English.

items.example: Can I change money at this bank?
items.note: At a bank, change money means exchange money into another currency. Money is uncountable.

items.example: I need to get money from the bank.
items.note: In this context, get money from a cash machine means withdraw cash, not necessarily earn money.

items.example: I'll post a letter after work.
items.note: Post can be a verb meaning send by mail, especially in British English; mail a letter is also common.

items.example: She went to post a parcel.
items.note: To post a parcel means to send a package through the postal service. Parcel is a countable noun.

items.example: You can park your car near the library.
items.note: Park can be a verb. You can park your car in a car park or in another place where parking is permitted.

items.example: We can get a train to Oxford.
items.note: You can get a train at a train or railway station. Catch a train and take a train are also possible.

items.example: You can get a bus from the station.
items.note: Get a bus means take or catch a bus. The textbook distinguishes a bus station from a railway station.

items.example: Follow the EXIT sign to leave the building.
items.note: On a public sign, EXIT shows the way out of a building. It is the opposite of entrance.

items.example: The entrance is on the left.
items.note: An entrance is the place where you go into a building or an area. Compare the EXIT sign.

items.example: The café has a No smoking sign.
items.note: This notice means smoking is not allowed here. No + -ing is common on prohibition signs.

items.example: The ticket machine is out of order today.
items.note: If a machine is out of order, it is not working. This notice is used for a broken cash machine in the exercises.

items.pt: Por favor, não pise na grama
items.example: The sign in the park says, “Please keep off the grass.”
items.note: A polite notice asking people not to walk on or enter the grass. Keep off is a phrasal verb.

items.section: C · Asking for and giving directions
items.example: Where is the bus station, please?
items.note: A direct question about the location of a place. Add please to make the request more polite.

items.section: C · Asking for and giving directions
items.example: How do I get to the town hall?
items.note: Use How do I get to + a place? to ask for directions. The example supplies the destination for natural pronunciation.
items.speechText: How do I get to the station?

items.section: C · Asking for and giving directions
items.example: Is there a bank near here?
items.note: Use Is there a/an + singular place + near here? to ask whether a service is nearby.
items.speechText: Is there a bank near here?

items.section: C · Asking for and giving directions
items.example: Can I park here after six?
items.note: Can I ...? asks about permission or possibility. A local sign may show whether parking is permitted.

items.section: C · Asking for and giving directions
items.example: Excuse me, where is the library?
items.note: A polite way to start a question when asking a stranger for directions.

items.section: C · Asking for and giving directions
items.example: I'm looking for the museum.
items.note: Look for means try to find someone or something. Follow the phrase with a destination or object.

items.word: Can you tell me the way to...?
items.pt: Pode me dizer o caminho para...?
items.ipa: /kæn juː tel miː ðə weɪ tuː/
items.section: C · Asking for and giving directions
items.example: Can you tell me the way to the nearest bank?
items.note: A polite way to ask for directions; use to followed by a specific destination.
items.speechText: Can you tell me the way to the bank?

items.section: C · Asking for and giving directions
items.example: Where is the nearest post office?
items.note: The superlative of near. The nearest bank is the bank closest to you.

items.section: C · Asking for and giving directions
items.example: Go left here and continue to the end of the road.
items.note: An instruction to travel towards the left. In many situations, turn left is also natural.

items.section: C · Asking for and giving directions
items.example: Go right after the bridge.
items.note: A simple instruction to move towards the right. Turn right is often clearer at a road junction.

items.section: C · Asking for and giving directions
items.example: Turn right at the bank.
items.note: Change direction towards the right. Compare on the right, which describes a place rather than an action.

items.section: C · Asking for and giving directions
items.example: Turn left at the end of the road.
items.note: Change direction towards the left. Compare on the left, which describes a location.

items.word: at the end of the road
items.section: C · Asking for and giving directions
items.example: The station is at the end of the road.
items.note: This phrase identifies a location near the point where a road finishes. Use at, not in.

items.section: C · Asking for and giving directions
items.example: Take the first right after the station.
items.note: Turn into the first road on the right. First is an ordinal number.

items.section: C · Asking for and giving directions
items.example: Take the second left to reach the bank.
items.note: Turn into the second road on the left. Second is an ordinal number.

items.section: C · Asking for and giving directions
items.example: The entrance is on the left.
items.note: Use this to say where something is. It is different from turn left, an instruction to change direction.

items.section: C · Asking for and giving directions
items.example: The museum is on the right.
items.note: Use this to locate something on the right-hand side. Compare turn right for giving an instruction.

items.word: on the other side of the road
items.ipa: /ɒn ði ˌʌðə saɪd əv ðə ˈrəʊd/
items.section: C · Asking for and giving directions
items.example: The library is on the other side of the road.
items.note: The other side of the road is opposite the side where you are standing.

items.section: C · Asking for and giving directions
items.example: Take the number 31 bus to the centre.
items.note: Use take the number + route number + bus to specify a bus service. Read 31 as thirty-one.

items.section: C · Asking for and giving directions
items.example: Get off at the next stop.
items.note: A phrasal verb meaning leave a bus, train or similar vehicle. The opposite is get on.

items.section: C · Asking for and giving directions
items.example: Get off at the second stop.
items.note: This gives the stop where you should get off. Second is an ordinal number.

items.section: C · Asking for and giving directions
items.example: There is a bank on Market Street.
items.note: Use there is for one thing or uncountable nouns; use there are for plural countable nouns.

items.section: C · Asking for and giving directions
items.example: Can you show me the way?
items.note: In directions, way means route or path. It can also mean method, as in a way to learn.

items.section: C · Asking for and giving directions
items.example: The museum is on Bridge Road.
items.note: A road is a route for vehicles. In an address, Road is capitalised as part of a proper street name.

items.section: C · Asking for and giving directions
items.example: The shop is on Market Street.
items.note: A street is a road, usually in a town or city. Capitalise Street in a name such as Market Street.

items.word: get off at the second stop
items.section: C · Asking for and giving directions
items.example: Get off at the second stop after the museum.
items.note: Get off at + a bus stop is the complete direction used in the teaching dialogue; second tells you which stop.

learningObjectives: Identify familiar places in town, such as the station, bank, tourist information office, library, town hall and car park, and explain their functions.
Understand the displayed public notices: exit, entrance, no smoking, out of order and please keep off the grass.
Ask for directions using Where is, How do I get to, Is there ... near here, and Can you tell me the way to.
Follow and give directions on a town map using go left, turn right, take the first right, take the second left, and location phrases.
Explain how to take a numbered bus, get off at a stop and give polite directions to local services.

units.title: Unit 30 — In the countryside
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use Elementary, 3rd ed., Unit 30, textbook pp. 66–67 (PDF pp. 67–68); original example sentences.

items.example: I enjoy spending weekends in the countryside.
items.note: The countryside means areas outside towns and cities. Say in the countryside, not in nature. The phonemic index gives /ˈkʌntrɪsaɪd/.

items.example: My grandparents live in the country.
items.note: Country may mean a nation, such as Brazil, or rural areas when used in the country. Context matters.

items.example: We climbed a mountain last summer.
items.note: The singular form of mountains, which is labelled in the picture. A mountain is generally higher than a hill.

items.example: There is snow on the mountains.
items.note: Mountains is the plural of mountain. The lesson uses in the mountains with walking and skiing.

items.example: The house stands on a hill.
items.note: The singular of hills, which appears in the picture. A hill is usually lower than a mountain.

items.example: The village lies between two hills.
items.note: The plural of hill. Hills are raised areas of land, generally smaller than mountains.

items.example: We walked through the forest.
items.note: A large area covered mainly by trees. The same illustration contrasts forest with a smaller wood.

items.example: There is a small wood near our house.
items.note: Here, a wood is a small area of trees. Wood also means the material that trees provide.

items.example: We walked in the woods.
items.note: A plural form commonly used to describe an area with many trees. It appears in the descriptive exercises.

items.example: We swam in the lake.
items.note: An area of water surrounded by land. The exercises mention going swimming in a lake.

items.example: The cows are in the field.
items.note: An area of land on a farm, often used for growing crops or keeping animals. The plural is fields.

items.example: The farmer works in the fields.
items.note: The plural of field. The textbook uses work in the fields, not work on the fields.

items.example: There is a path through the wood.
items.note: A narrow route for walking. You can walk along a path through the countryside.

items.example: The river flows past the village.
items.note: A large natural stream of flowing water. People may have a picnic by a river.

items.example: They live on a farm.
items.note: A place where crops or animals are produced. Say live on a farm, not live in a farm.

items.example: We drove along a quiet country road.
items.note: A road in a rural area. The label appears in the landscape illustration.

items.example: The village has about eight hundred people.
items.note: A small settlement in the countryside. The textbook contrasts a village with a small town.

items.example: She moved to a small town.
items.note: A town smaller than a large city but generally bigger than a village. The population figures in the book are illustrative, not fixed rules.

items.example: The farmer works outside every day.
items.note: Someone who works on a farm, often growing food or raising animals.

items.example: My uncle lives on a farm.
items.note: Use on with farm: live on a farm, not live in a farm.

items.example: They work in the fields in summer.
items.note: Use in with fields when describing a farmer working in those areas.

items.example: We stayed in a cottage near the village.
items.note: A small house, especially in a village or in the countryside.

items.example: I love nature.
items.note: Nature means the natural world. In the general meaning, say I love nature, not I love the nature.

items.example: Conservation is important for wildlife.
items.note: The protection of the natural environment, animals and plants. It is an uncountable noun in this sense.

items.example: We saw wonderful wildlife in the national park.
items.note: Wild animals living in nature, including birds, fish and insects. Unlike nature, wildlife does not usually include plants.

items.example: The forest is a conservation area.
items.note: A place where the natural environment and wildlife are protected. It is not necessarily the same as a national park.

items.example: We went walking in a national park.
items.note: A large protected natural area. Say in a national park when referring to a location.

items.word: in the north of the country
items.example: There are many forests in the north of the country.
items.note: A location in the northern part of a nation; the country here means the nation, not rural land.

items.word: in the south of the country
items.example: It is warmer in the south of the country.
items.note: A location in the southern part of a nation; south contrasts with north.

items.example: Many animals live in the forest.
items.note: Animal is a countable noun; animals is its plural. It is listed as part of nature in the source explanation.

items.example: We watched birds near the lake.
items.note: Birds is the plural of bird. The textbook lists birds among wildlife.

items.example: These plants grow near the river.
items.note: Plants are living things such as grass, trees and flowers. They are part of nature but not wildlife in the book’s definition.

items.example: There are fish in the river.
items.note: Fish is commonly both singular and plural. The book includes fish in its examples of wildlife.

items.example: Many insects live in the wood.
items.note: Insects is the plural of insect. It is one of the wildlife categories identified by the textbook.

items.example: I love nature because I enjoy spending time outdoors.
items.note: The example teaches zero article: I love nature, not I love the nature.

items.example: We walk in the countryside on Sundays.
items.note: Say walk in the countryside or walk in a natural area. Avoid walk in the nature.

items.example: We had a picnic by the lake.
items.note: A common collocation meaning eat a meal outdoors. You can have a picnic by a river or in a park.

items.example: We go walking in the forest.
items.note: Use go + -ing for many leisure activities: go walking, go swimming and go skiing.

items.example: They go skiing in the mountains.
items.note: A winter-sports collocation using go + -ing. The textbook associates skiing with mountains.

items.example: We go swimming in the lake when the weather is warm.
items.note: An activity collocation reinforced by the exercise about swimming in a lake.

items.example: We walked along a path for an hour.
items.note: Walk along means follow a route, such as a path. The expression is reinforced by exercise 30.3.

items.example: They skied down the mountain.
items.note: Down indicates movement towards a lower place. The exercise pairs skiing with movement down a mountain.

items.example: We sat by the river to eat.
items.note: By means beside or near. This phrase is based on the picnic scene in exercise 30.3.

items.example: We saw some wildlife in the national park.
items.note: Wildlife means animals in their natural surroundings; the exercise practises seeing wildlife in a national park.

items.example: We sometimes go swimming in the lake in summer.
items.note: This activity-and-place pattern is practised in exercise 30.3, which links swimming with the lake.

items.pt: fazer uma caminhada por uma trilha
items.example: They go walking along a path through the forest.
items.note: Use go walking for the activity and along to describe following a path. This combination is reinforced in exercise 30.3.

learningObjectives: Name the countryside features in the illustration, including mountains, hills, a forest, a wood, a lake, fields, a path, a river and a farm.
Distinguish a village from a small town and use the collocations live on a farm, work in the fields and live in a cottage.
Explain the countryside / the country versus a country distinction and avoid incorrect articles with nature and wildlife.
Understand nature, wildlife, a conservation area and a national park, including the difference between plants and wildlife.
Describe rural activities with have a picnic, go walking, go swimming, go skiing, and prepositions for paths, rivers and mountains.
